**ID:** Ja 362
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1

**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

In the narrative framework, the Buddha delivers the teaching while staying at the Jetavana monastery regarding a brahmin who wished to test the power and comparative value of moral virtue (*sīla*) [Fausböll 1883]. In the past story (introduced with the verse incipit *Sīlaṁ seyyo*), the king holds the protagonist in high regard for his virtue beyond other brahmins [Fausböll 1883]. To determine whether virtue or learning is more valuable, the Bodhisatta takes a coin each day until he is arrested on the third day, thereby proving the supremacy of virtue over mere learning [Anandajoti 2010].
